newsitem.title: UK: US rate fears, Russia occupy emerging markets.
newsitem.headline: US rate fears, Russia occupy emerging markets.

text.p: Prospects for the passage of Russia's 1997 budget and Kazakhstan's plans for a debt Eurobond will preoccupy emerging market investors this week, but worries over U.S. interest rates are likely to take centre stage.
U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan sparked a sharp sell-off in global markets last week when he said investors must be wary of "irrational exuberance."
His comments renewed fears that U.S. interest rates may have to rise, giving the Brady market a nasty jolt and hitting emerging stock markets.
One emerging market economist said he saw the impact on the emerging markets continuing, although world stock and bond markets calmed on Monday and began to recoup some of their losses.
News late on Friday that Russia's Duma had postponed its vote on the draft 1997 budget until December 15 helped depress Russian debt prices. But some investors were sanguine.

"For those who have been following Russia closely the postponement of the vote will come as no surprise. It was widely expected," said Charles Blitzer, chief economist for emerging markets at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette.
"There is a good chance of the budget passing its first reading in December but clearly it is not going to get through its final reading until next year."
Successful passage in mid-December will help Russian debt prices recover.
Fixed income investors will also be keeping a close eye on events in Bulgaria.

Two International Monetary Fund technical missions arrive in the east European country this week to assist Sofia adjusts its 1997 budget frame to fit the needs of its proposed currency board, which may be introduced in January.
The plans are expected to help revive the country's flagging stock market, but some investors are worried about the Bulgaria's beleagured currency and its impact on inflation.
"Bulgaria seems to be getting closer to the brink of hyperinflation. We will be looking very carefully at the exchange rate development this week," said a London-based eastern European economist.
"The concern stems from rapid depreciation of the exchange rate, which dropped by 20 percent last week," he said.

Further east, Kazakhstan is expected to launch its debut Eurobond early next week. Though few details were available, the market consensus is centring on a likely $200 million three-year issue priced about three percentage points over U.S. Treasuries.

Jordan will keep Middle Eastern investors on their toes after Iraq said on Friday it intended to resume oil exports this week following its agreement to U.N. conditions that will allow a delayed oil-for-food deal to go ahead.
"I think we are going to see more institutional buying and more individuals participating in the market," said Basir Siman, director of Middle East and North Africa equity research at UBS.

He said the Jordanian market would be buoyant because sceptical players who stayed on the sidelines last week were now reassured that the deal, which allows Iraq to sell $2 billion of oil over six months, would go ahead.
Egypt's stock market may see some profit-taking by domestic investors this week, while Morocco will continue its gradual market consolidation, Siman added.
Latin American markets are expected to be quiet in the run-up to the Christmas holidays, with the focus mainly on Argentina and Chile.
Ondine Smulders, Latin America strategist at James Capel, said that Argentina was likely to maintain its good economic performance until the end of 1996.
"At the moment, Argentina is basically on a very good run," she said. "You are going to get continued good news on the economy and pension funds will be putting more money into the equity market."
Smulders said investors in Chile would concentrate on the electricity sector whose stocks have tumbled in recent weeks.
They have been hit by poor company results and fears of higher generating costs as drought conditions hit Chile's hydro-electric companies.

Economic figures released by the government indicated the economy was slowing down, she said, adding that was an expectation that the central bank would cut interest rates by 25 basis points, probably next year.

Investors will also be awaiting Brazil's November import figures after export numbers were announced last week. A government official said November's trade deficit was likely to be lower than October's record $1.3 billion.
The IFC emerging market composite investable index, IFC/IPRD, denominated in dollars, was up 0.4 percent week on week at 295.95 points on Friday.
Latin America was up 2.2 percent at 534.93, Asia was down 0.4 at 254.98, and Europe, Middle East and Africa was down 0.8 at 134.96.
